instructions:
Build a change calendar.
Who it is for: a team that keeps deploying into someone else's launch.
What it must do:
- Record planned changes with owner, blast radius and rollback plan.
- Warn when two changes to the same system land on the same day.
- Support a freeze window.
- Show whose change collides with whose.
Done when: two changes to the same system on one day raise a warning, and a freeze cannot be booked over without a recorded reason.
Nobody can book over a freeze without stating a reason, and the reason is kept.

Features it must ship with (each of these is part of done, not a stretch):
- Conflict detection: Two changes touching the same service in the same window are flagged when they are scheduled, not after.
- Freeze windows: Declare a period where nothing ships; anything scheduled into it is blocked with the reason shown.
- On-call context: Every change shows who is holding the pager during its window, so the person who will be woken knows it exists.
- Retrospective view: Filter to a time range and see exactly what changed — the first question of every incident.
- Subscribable feed: An iCal feed per service or team, so it lives in the calendar people already look at.

Screens: Calendar, Schedule a change, Service view, Freeze windows.

Quality bar — this is the difference between a demo and something usable:
- Every list has a designed empty state that says what to do next, not a blank panel.
- Every destructive action is confirmable and reversible, or it is not …
why: New app from scratch; it schedules deployments as data but does not touch any deployment config.

instructions:
Build a documentation freshness board.
Who it is for: whoever owns docs nobody trusts any more.
What it must do:
- Read a docs folder from a repository.
- For each page show last edited, the code paths it mentions, and whether those have changed since.
- Sort by most likely to be wrong.
- Let a page be marked reviewed, which resets its clock.
Done when: a page whose referenced code changed ranks above one whose did not, and marking it reviewed moves it down.
Likely-wrong is computed, not a status somebody has to remember to set.

Features it must ship with (each of these is part of done, not a stretch):
- Staleness, computed not guessed: Each page's age is compared against the last change to the code paths it mentions — a doc is stale relative to its subject, not to the calendar.
- Code references extracted: Paths, symbols and commands are pulled out of each page and linked, so you can see what a page claims to describe.
- Ranked worklist: Sorted most-likely-wrong first, with the reason shown, so an afternoon spent on it is spent well.
- Mark reviewed: Confirming a page is still correct resets its clock and records who checked — the difference between old and unverified.
- Trend over time: One number for the whole set, so a team can see whether the rot is getting better or worse.

Screens: Repository connect, Freshness board, Page detail with references, Trend.

title:

instructions:
Build a lead triage inbox.
Who it is for: a small team drowning in inbound that is mostly noise.
What it must do:
- Take a batch of enquiries and score each on fit against a profile you define.
- Draft a first reply for the good ones and a polite decline for the rest.
- Queue them for one-click send.
- Keep the fit profile as editable text.
Done when: every enquiry gets a score and a draft, and nothing leaves the queue without a click.
Nothing sends without a human pressing send.

Features it must ship with (each of these is part of done, not a stretch):
- An ICP you can edit: Industries, budget, keywords and any other dimension you add — stored as data, so tuning who qualifies is an edit rather than a deploy.
- Explainable scoring: Every score shows the tokens that earned it and what each was worth. A number nobody can interrogate gets ignored.
- Drafted replies, two tones: Accept and decline drafts generated per lead, with a tone control, and the decline carries a disclaimer that cannot be edited out.
- Human gate: Nothing sends without an explicit review tick. The approver, the timestamp and a hash of what was sent are recorded.
- Audit trail: Append-only log of every send, exportable — the thing you need when somebody asks what was said in March.

Screens: ICP editor, Inbox with scores, Draft review, Audit log.

title:
Build an incident timeline builder.
Who it is for: an on-call enginee…
instructions:
Build an incident timeline builder.
Who it is for: an on-call engineer writing the post-mortem the morning after.
What it must do:
- Take an alert log and a chat transcript and lay them on one timeline.
- Mark detection, escalation, mitigation and all-clear; compute time-to-detect and time-to-resolve.
- Let a human correct every milestone the tool proposes.
- Export a markdown post-mortem with the timeline embedded.
Done when: a real incident log produces a timeline with all four milestones and both durations, and the exported markdown opens cleanly.
Storage is one JSON file per incident, so it can live in the repo beside the code.

Features it must ship with (each of these is part of done, not a stretch):
- Two sources, one timeline: Paste an alert log and a chat export; both are parsed, timestamped and merged into a single ordered spine with the source shown on every entry.
- Milestones you can argue with: Detection, escalation, mitigation and all-clear are proposed from the evidence — and every one can be moved, with the tool showing which line it inferred it from.
- Durations that recompute: Time-to-detect and time-to-resolve update live as milestones move, so a correction costs a drag rather than a rewrite.
- Gap detection: Stretches with no activity are flagged: the twenty silent minutes are usually the finding, and they are invisible in a raw log.
- Markdown export: One post-mortem file with the timeline embedded, the durations stated, and every claim linked to the log …
why: New app from scratch storing JSON per incident; no sensitive surface.

title: URL slug generator
instructions: Create slugify.py with a function slugify(text: str) -> str that converts arbitrary text into a URL slug: lowercase, spaces and consecutive whitespace collapse to single hyphens, non-alphanumeric characters (other than hyphens) are removed, leading/trailing hyphens stripped, and consecutive hyphens collapsed. Unicode letters are transliterated to ASCII when possible via unicodedata NFKD, otherwise dropped.
acceptance_criteria: slugify('Hello, World!') == 'hello-world'
slugify('  a  b  ') == 'a-b'
slugify('Crème brûlée') == 'creme-brulee'
slugify('---') == '' and slugify('') == ''

title: Token-bucket rate limiter
instructions: Create rate_limiter.py with a class TokenBucket(capacity: int, refill_per_second: float, clock=None). Method allow(n: int = 1) -> bool consumes n tokens if available and returns True, else False without consuming. Tokens refill continuously based on elapsed time from the injectable clock callable (defaults to time.monotonic), never exceeding capacity. Reject non-positive capacity/refill at construction with ValueError; allow(n<=0) raises ValueError.
acceptance_criteria: A fresh bucket with capacity 3 allows exactly 3 single-token calls, then denies
Advancing the injected clock refills proportionally and caps at capacity
Constructor and allow() validate their inputs with ValueError
why: Creates a new module from scratch, though a small, fully specified one that some would treat as tier 1.

title: CSV sales aggregation

Return {'total_revenue': float, 'by_region': {region: revenue}, 'top_region': str|None} where revenue = units * unit_price summed. Skip rows with missing/blank region or non-numeric units/unit_price (do not raise). top_region is None for empty input; ties break alphabetically.
acceptance_criteria: Malformed rows are skipped, not fatal
Ties on revenue pick the alphabetically first region
Empty input returns zero revenue, empty by_region, top_region None

title: Markdown table-of-contents generator
instructions: Create md_toc.py with a function toc(markdown: str, max_depth: int = 3) -> str. Parse ATX headings (#, ##, ... up to max_depth), ignore headings inside fenced code blocks (``` ... ```), and emit a nested bullet list where each entry is '- [title](#anchor)' indented two spaces per level below the top. Anchors: lowercase, spaces to hyphens, strip characters other than word chars and hyphens. Duplicate anchors get -1, -2 suffixes in order of appearance.
acceptance_criteria: Headings inside fenced code blocks are ignored
Anchor generation matches the rules incl. duplicate suffixing
max_depth limits which heading levels appear
why: Creates a new module from scratch, though a small, fully specified one that some would treat as tier 1.

why: Changes who can access data.

title: Manual approval for prod deploys
instructions: Change the GitHub Actions workflow so merges to main no longer deploy to prod automatically; require a manual approval step.
why: Deployment pipeline configuration change.

title: Sales tax at checkout
instructions: Add US sales tax to the checkout total based on the shipping state.
why: Changes the amount charged, which is a payment flow; it reads like an ordinary feature.

title: Expense reimbursement app
instructions:
Build an expense reimbursement app.
Who it is for: a 40-person company doing this in spreadsheets.
What it must do:
- Employees submit receipts with amount and category.
- Their manager approves or rejects; finance can see everything.
- Approved expenses export as a bank transfer batch file.
Done when: an employee cannot see anyone else's claims and nothing is exported without manager approval.
why: A new build whose core is role-based access and a payout money flow, so the sensitive surface decides over tier 2.

title: Regenerate API key
instructions: On the settings page, show API keys masked (last 4 chars only) and add a 'Regenerate' button that revokes the old key.
why: Regenerating and revoking credentials changes a credential surface; the masking alone would be tier 0.
